speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The borrowings under SINGA are clearly distinguishable from a separate category of Government borrowing for non-spending purposes under the Local Treasury Bills Act, or LTBA, and the Government Securities Act, or the GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The LTBA and the GSA allow the Government to borrow, not for spending, but for specific purposes, such as market development and meeting the investment needs of the Central Provident Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To emphasise, the proceeds from such borrowings cannot be spent by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, to delineate between the two types of borrowing in legislation, the borrowings which are done under SINGA for SINGA projects and borrowings which cannot be spent, this Bill before the House seeks to merge the LTBA into the GSA, and to streamline our legislation on Government borrowings.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will help to provide better clarity on the profile of the Government's debt.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The LTBA authorises the issuance of Treasury Bills to develop the domestic short-term debt market and to meet market demand for short-term Government debt securities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The GSA authorises the issuance of longer-tenor securities, like the Singapore Government Securities, or SGS, to develop the domestic debt market and meet the investment needs of the Central Provident Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both the LTBA and the GSA expressly provide that the proceeds of borrowings raised are to be paid into the Government Securities Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an important safeguard, because the monies in the Government Securities Fund can only be invested.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is why the monies raised under the LTBA and GSA cannot be used to finance the Government's spending needs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While the LTBA and GSA were introduced separately with different processes, the Government has gradually harmonised the treatment of Treasury Bills and SGS over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the LTBA was amended in 1996 to account for the proceeds and expenditures of Treasury Bills under the Government Securities Fund, instead of the Consolidated Fund, similar to Government securities in the GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In 2001, the minimum denomination for Treasury Bills of $10,000 was revised downwards to $1,000 to facilitate greater retail participation, similar to that for tradable securities under the GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in 2004, the GSA was amended to change the borrowing limit of Government securities issued from a gross to a net limit for a more meaningful measure of Government's liabilities, similar to that for Treasury Bills under the LTBA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, given the overlaps in purpose and the harmonisation of treatment of securities under both Acts, this Bill is therefore introduced to merge the LTBA into the GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government Securities Act will be renamed as the Government Securities (Debt Market and Investment) Act, which I will refer to as the renamed GSA for short, to reflect this consolidation within the name of the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The renamed GSA will provide for the issuance of Treasury Bills and the existing LTBA will be repealed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The changes introduced through this Bill are largely administrative in nature with no change to the substance of the individual Acts.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is no change to the provision, limiting the use of monies in the Government Securities Fund from being used solely for investment purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Therefore, the monies raised under the Bill cannot be used for spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is no change to the overall borrowing limit.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As is the practice today, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will continue to calibrate Treasury Bill and SGS issuances based on market development needs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And to ensure transparency, MAS will continue to publish the breakdown of outstanding SGS and Treasury Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is also no change to the existing features and outstanding issuances of Treasury Bills and Government Securities issued under the LTBA and the GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The outstanding Treasury Bills will be automatically subsumed under the renamed GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides the merging of LTBA into the GSA, this Bill will also repeal borrowing provisions in other Acts that are no longer necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are no outstanding borrowings under these Acts.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, with the SINGA and renamed GSA, the Government does not foresee the need to borrow under these Acts.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Constitution and other acts, such as the MAS Act will be amended to substitute references to LTBA and GSA with the renamed GSA, and remove references to the External Loans Act.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments to the Constitution will be raised by the Minister for Law after this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have consulted the President on both this Bill and the amendments to the Constitution, as they provide for the raising of loans by the Government and a single borrowing limit for Government securities and Treasury Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This Bill consolidates various pieces of legislation on Government borrowings for specific non-spending purposes into a single legislation under the renamed GSA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will ensure that the borrowings for spending and non-spending purposes are transparent and clearly differentiated in the processes for the issuances of securities, reporting and public communications.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And again, I would like to emphasise that the Singapore Government has a strong balance sheet with no net debt.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, the Government's balance sheet has indeed expanded and hence, it does make good sense do some "housekeeping" to the various Government borrowing legislations, and in particular, this Bill to consolidate the GSA and LTBA as well as make consequential amendments and repeals to the other Acts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister for the basis of this change?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The reasons for my question are as follows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Both debts come with different tenures, repayment obligations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Treasury Bills tend to be more liquid in the trading markets because it is shorter dated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, from the credit market standpoint, the two debts, say, the three-month Treasury Bill versus 20-year SGS would be accorded with different risk ratings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Does MOF see the need to retain this separate borrowing limits for these two buckets of issuances given that they both have different risk profile?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is issued to CPF Board so that the Government can pay the bond coupon rates to the CPF members, which match the interest that CPF members receive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These bonds are not traded in the market and are directly placed with CPF.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, this is not for the purpose of creating high quality liquid assets for the financial institutions or to build a domestic risk-free yield curve, as opposed to the purpose of SGS.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Because of its sheer size, this SSGS, and that it will continue to grow in tandem with higher wages and growth in our resident workforce, we can expect the SSGS to get even more sizeable as the CPF savings increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the SSGS is aggregated with the SGS, the overall debt level of the Government will come across as very high relative to our GDP and give the impression that a lot more SGS is issued or traded in the market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These would give greater clarity to the market participants and analysts on the level of the borrowing by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is fairly obscure, so obscure, in fact, that I noticed that, initially, I was the only Member slated to speak on this but evidently, two others have since found this topic similarly irresistible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I favour such simplification and I do not have substantive concerns about the specificities in the proposed amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do wish, however, to make a few points that I think have more to do with potentially unintended consequences of the current iteration of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These have to do with the debt limit precluding the acceptance of advance deposits by the MAS for Treasury Bills and the lack of justification for rejecting sales.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This new limit may then be increased by Parliamentary resolution, which simplifies, since logically, all forms of debt, whether short-term or long-term should, of course, be treated as a component of the overall liability picture and, hence, subject to the same form of debt ceiling discipline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given this observation, would it not also make sense to enfold remaining instruments under Government borrowing, such as single bonds issued under the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act to the same limit?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand, of course, as Minister Wong has mentioned that this is, in fact, a separate accounting convention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This limit, to be clear, is relatively small, at $90 billion and there is a clear benefit through consolidating under one roof, which is that a consolidated limit would simplify monitoring and allow fiscal policy-makers to ultimately focus on the single figure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the natural objection, of course, is this, is that the Government maintains these separate limits for debt that serve developmental objectives, such as infrastructure, which is the case for SINGA versus those issued under risk transfer and investment purposes for the purposes of CPF funds as mentioned earlier, or to fulfil liquidity and debt functions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOF has steadfastly held that all these require separate limit accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But from the perspective of understanding the underlying economics, all monies is ultimately fungible and it is unclear why debt issued under one type of accounting constraint cannot subsequently be redeployed to other functions so long as it is only a matter of protocol, rather than one entrenched in actual legislation that prevents subsequent transfer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, such deviations need not occur under this Government but it could easily occur under another perhaps more profligate one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, even if we did wish to maintain separate debt ceilings for the purposes of accounting, perhaps it may be worth nevertheless incorporating these distinct limits into this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially the case since insofar as financial markets are concerned, they view the consolidated Government balance sheet as a whole, as they should.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, SINGA bonds do not appear to have affected the Singapore Government's overall credit rating, which is yet another economic reason to not hive off such limits for the instrument.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Concomitantly, it is also important to calibrate the frequency with which this limit is modified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this effect, may I inquire whether this Government has considered whether this limit is appropriate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is the premise or justification behind the current debt limit ceiling amount of $1.065 trillion?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Is there a body that routinely examines the veracity of this debt limit and how frequently should we expect to change this?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this may be a sound principle in practice, history is rife with examples of central banks that have gone ahead and monetised debt on behalf of a profligate sovereign, breeding inflation as a result.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is worth noting that two recent developments may yet necessitate additional flexibility for the monetary authority to act in an anticipatory manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first such circumstance, as Members of this House would be aware of, has to do with the zero lower bound faced by nominal interest rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although Singapore has never quite faced this problem in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis of 2007/2008 and the MAS, unlike most central banks, targets the nominal exchange rate rather than the policy interest rate, it is nevertheless worth keeping in mind that one prescription to the problem of the zero lower bound is to allow for central banks to intervene directly in short-term money markets by issuing securities on their own account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The second situation is to do with the emerging central bank digital currency landscape (CBDC).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such CBDCs are likely to become a permanent part of the future of central banking worldwide and I understand that MAS is on the forefront of this and even commissioned the sandbox for studying the usage of such currencies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the merging of limits under the Government Securities Act and the Local Treasury Bills Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern is that we currently have a much higher borrowing limit for Government securities than for Treasury Bills – more than nine times as much.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government had its rationale for maintaining this disparity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I have three related questions: One, what was the initial intent of having a much higher borrowing limit for Government Securities and Treasury Bills?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry see this initial intent as no longer relevant, given that this intent is no longer reflected in the combined borrowing limit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, will this combined limit now result in a greater reliance on Treasury Bills compared to Government securities?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three, will the Government internally maintain a separate borrowing limit for Government Securities and Treasury Bills?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both the existing section 11 and the new section 11 allows the Government to borrow beyond its limit as long as there is a Parliamentary resolution and presidential concurrence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In both cases, all the Government needs is for the Parliament to pass a resolution by simple majority and for the President to concur.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the borrowing limit merely meant to signal the Government's stance on maximum borrowing?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Relatedly, will the Ministry consider introducing a strengthened check-and-balance for when the Government seeks to increase its borrowing limit or to borrow beyond the existing limit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we could require such activities to require a two-third vote of approval by the Parliament in addition to the President's concurrence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This process change would reflect the sanctity of the borrowing limit and the severity of increasing or bypassing it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa said, it is housekeeping.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no change to the substance of our borrowing legislation, the overall borrowing limit and the safeguards to raising the current limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But let me clarify some of the questions and points that Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the outstanding amount of securities under the Local Treasury Bills Act (LTBA) and the Government Securities Act (GSA).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Louis Ng also asked about the rationale for merging the LTBA and GSA borrowing limits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, with the introduction of SINGA, we thought that it would be timely to consolidate legislation of Government borrowings for non-spending purposes so as to distinguish these from borrowing for spending purposes under SINGA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By pooling the LTBA and the GSA together under the renamed GSA, this will emphasise that the borrowings issued under this Act are entirely for non-spending purposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This would also address what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim was saying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is prudent and advisable to have different limits for both.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Between GSA and LTBA, both are borrowing for non-spending reasons – one for short-term securities, another for longer-term securities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we felt that there is no need to distinguish so much between the two.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Furthermore, over time, the processes for treatment of LTBA and Treasury Bills and Government securities have become harmonised over the years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Therefore, we see scope for pooling them together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, a combined limit under this renamed GSA will also provide MAS greater flexibility to calibrate the issuances and tenors of debt issuances based on market conditions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, other countries such as the US and Germany similarly manage their short and long-tenor securities under a single limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With this combined borrowing limit, we do not expect the proportion of short- and long-term securities under the renamed GSA to be significantly different from today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is because a large proportion will continue to be used to issue Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS), which is mainly driven by CPF balances and its investment needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa has correctly highlighted, the amount of SSGS issuances is expected to increase over time due to growth in our resident labour force and wages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The remaining borrowing limit will mostly be utilised by the issuance of Treasury Bills and Singapore Government Securities (SGS) to support market development and it is market demand and conditions that will influence the amount and the tenor of such debt to be issued.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In particular, MAS will calibrate the amount and tenor of such issuances to meet the regulatory needs of financial institutions for high quality liquid assets and to establish a robust sovereign yield curve to support the development of the Singapore dollar corporate bond market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, it will not be in the Government's interest to issue debt of certain tenors beyond what the market can reasonably absorb as it would skew the interest rate curve used to price Singapore dollar denominated financial instruments and result in capital misallocations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, to reiterate again, we are combining all the borrowings that are for non-spending purposes – CPF, market development – pooling them together under this renamed GSA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We believe it is prudent and, from a financial point of view, provides better control – to have this differentiated from borrowing for SINGA projects, which is borrowing which will be used for financing of actual projects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That will be governed separately under SINGA and with a separate limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On Mr Liang Eng Hwa's suggestion for a separate borrowing limit for SSGS, I think he highlighted the need to provide clarity to market participants and analysts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Here, we do not believe there is a need for a separate limit – to carve out SSGS – because if the purpose is to provide clarity and transparency, indeed, the composition of borrowing, be it SSGS, SGS or Treasury Bills, this will be published and will be subject to public and parliamentary scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS will continue to publish monthly the breakdown of outstanding SGS and Treasury Bills that are issued.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, Mr Louis Ng asked about the purpose of this borrowing limit and if the governance over increases in borrowing limits could be further strengthened to reflect the sanctity of the borrowing limit and the severity of increasing or bypassing it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also alluded to this in his response.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is really nothing sacrosanct about the borrowing limits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, the Government reviews the borrowing limits periodically and we will come back to the Parliament to raise the limits through Parliamentary resolutions where required.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The most recent was in January this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, as demand for SSGS grows due to rising CPF balances, then, we will start to reach the limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Likewise, demand for SGS and Treasury Bills will change, depending on regulatory and investment needs and market conditions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What is important to understand is that the key safeguard, the key legislative safeguard in the Government Securities Act is that none of these borrowings can be spent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Like I said, it is differentiated from SINGA borrowings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Therefore, such borrowings do not lead to additional debt burdens.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Given that we already such a legislative safeguard under the GSA, some may ask why then is there still a need for a borrowing limit?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is useful for monitoring and each time we get close to the limit and we need to raise the limit, the Government would then have to come back to Parliament and get the agreement to raise this through Parliamentary resolution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thereafter, the President will act independently in her discretion to concur with this resolution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With the merger of the LTBA into the GSA, there will not be any change to the existing safeguards and processes that we have in place today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Clause 20 does not hinder us from effective monetary policy at all today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Clause 24 on the reserving the right to refuse a sale of debt to any entities, yes, that is in place in legislation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But should such a scenario were to arise, the Government will make clear its reasons for refusal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in any case, we will continue to review and update all aspects of legislations and should there be new developments in the marketplace or new requirements, we will periodically update legislation where necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In summary, Sir, this Bill seeks to provide clarity on the Government’s debt profile, and reflect that the majority of the Government borrowings will continue to be issued under the renamed GSA for non-spending purposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I assure Members of this House that our fiscal position remains strong with borrowings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will review our debt limits regularly to ensure that we continue to borrow within our means and remain in a net asset position.
